newsitem.title: UK: Trust the first casualty in MGAM soap opera.
newsitem.headline: Trust the first casualty in MGAM soap opera.

text.p: The relationship of trust between pension funds and the firms who manage their investments may be the first casualty of the row between Morgan Grenfell and its former fund manager Nicola Horlick, industry professionals say.

Horlick's acrimonious departure from investment firm MGAM last week, and the blaze of publicity that surrounded it, has done nothing to reassure the trustees in charge of the life savings of thousands of UK pensioners.

"The process as a whole has not been an edifying spectacle," Paul Haines, investment director at Sedgwick Noble Lowndes, the biggest advisor of pension fund clients in Britain said on Tuesday. "This is a deeply upsetting incident for trustees."

Pension fund trustees were dismayed at the public fall-out between Horlick and MGAM, and baffled at the abandonment of the code of discretion which normally governs the industry's affairs -- and which they expect in return for hefty management fees.
Some funds will be weighing the option of shifting fund managers, and just how feasible that might be.
Agreements with fund managers include provisions for ending a relationship quickly, but their hands may be tied by the costs involved.
"They can't change (fund managers) overnight -- that's the downside of this soap opera stuff," said one top pension fund consultant in London.
Haines said he was worried about the delicate relationship that allows trustees to rely on the professionalism of their asset managers and their commitment to putting client interests first.
"The Morgan Grenfell issue undermines the element of trust in that process and is to be regretted by the industry as a whole," Haines added.

News that the MGAM, which manages some 18.0 billion pounds ($30 billion) of UK pension fund money, had suspended Horlick shot a bolt of anxiety through its its pension fund clients. Her subsequent resignation did little to allay that unease.
Many had personal contact with Horlick and despite full cooperation from MGAM they felt powerless as events unfurled.
Pension funds at councils across Britain put their relationship with MGAM on watch and will decide what to do over a series of meetings in February and March.

"A decision will be taken on (March 4) as to whether to continue with the arrangements or offer (the fund's management) for retendering," an official at the London Borough of Lewisham, which has 300 million pounds in pension money under sole management with MGAM, told Reuters on Monday.
The transaction costs involved in reshaping a portfolio to suit a new fund manager's style, and the dealing costs in buying and selling shares, are the main deterrents.

"You can incur start-up costs of up to half a percent, which is quite substantial -- on a 100 million pound portfolio that would be half a million pounds," said one pension fund executive with assets under MGAM management.
"But if you are going to do something you need to do so quickly -- if you have an interregnum period of some sort, it means market opportunities will be missed."
Haines said the loss of trust the MGAM affair may have sparked could end up costing pension funds more as they vet fund managers and costs themselves.
"If the trustees feel they have to spend more time scrutinising managers, someone will have to pay for it," he said. "This will come out of the schemes, the companies or their members."
